source_text:
Viginti et duas litteras esse apud Hebræos, Syrorum quoque lingua et Chaldæorum testatur, quæ Hebræa magna ex parte confinis est. Nam et ipsi vigintiduo elementa habent eodem sono, sed diversis characteribus. Samaritani etiam Pentateuchum Moysi totidem litteris scriptitant, figuris tantum et apicibus discrepantes. Certumque est Esdram scribam, legisque doctorem, post captam Jerosolymam et instaurationem templi sub Zorobabel, alias litteras reperisse quibus nunc utimur, cum ad illud usque tempus iidem Samaritanorum et Hebræorum characteres fuerint. In libro quoque Numerorum hæc eadem supputatio, sub Levitarum, ac sacerdotum censu, mystice ostenditur.
Et nomen Domini tetragrammaton, in quibusdam Græcis voluminibus, usque hodie antiquis expressum litteris invenimus. Sed et psalmi, trigesimus sextus, et centesimus decimus, et centesimus undecimus, et centesimus decimus octavus, et centesimus quadragesimus quartus, quanquam diverso scribantur metro, tamen ejusdem numeri texuntur alphabeto. Et Jeremiæ lamentationes, et oratio ejus : Salomonis quoque in fine proverbia, ab eo loco in quo ait : Mulierem fortem quis inveniet ? iisdem alphabetis vel incisionibus supputantur. Porro quinque litteræ duplices apud Hebræos sunt, Caph, Mem, Nun, Pe, Sade, aliter enim scribuntur per has principia, medietatesque verborum, aliter fines. Unde et quinque a plerisque libri, duplices æstimantur, Samuel, Melachim, Dibre haiamim, Esdras, Jeremias, cum Cinoth, id est, lamentationibus suis. Quo modo igitur vigintiduo elementa sunt, per quæ scribimus Hebraice omne quod loquimur, et eorum initiis vox humana comprehenditur : ita viginti duo volumina supputantur, quibus quasi litteris et exordiis in Dei doctrina, tenera adhuc et lactens viri justi eruditur infantia.
Primus apud eos liber, vocatur בראסית Beresith : quem nos Genesim dicimus.
Secundus, ואלה סמות Veelle semoth : qui Exodus appellatur.
Tertius, ויקרא Vaiicra, id est Leviticus.
Quartus, וידבר Vajedabber, quem Numeros vocamus.
Quintus, אלה הדברים Elle haddebarim, qui Deuteronomium prænotatur. Hi sunt quinque libri Moysi, quos proprie תורה Thora, id est Legem appellant.
Secundum, prophetarum ordinem faciunt : et incipiunt ab Jesu filio Nave : qui apud eos יהוסע בן נון Josue ben Nun dicitur.
Deinde subtexunt סופטים Sophetim, id est Judicum librum. Et in eundem conpingunt Ruth : quia in diebus Judicum facta ejus narratur historia.
Tertius sequitur סמואל Samuel, quem nos Regum primum et secundum dicimus.
Quartus מלכים Melachim, id est Regum, quam ממלכות Mamlachot, id est Regnorum dicere. Non enim multarum gentium describit regna, sed unius Israelitici populi, qui tribubus duodecim continetur.
Quintus, est יסעיה Isaias.
Sextus, ירמיה Jeremias.
Septimus, יחזקאל Ezechiel.
Octavus, liber duodecim Prophetarum, : qui apud illos vocatur תרי עסר There asar.
Tertius ordo, Hagiographa possidet.
Et primus liber incipit a איוב Job.
Secundus a דוד David : quem quinque incisionibus, et uno Psalmorum volumine conprehendunt.
Tertius est סלמה Salomon, tres libros habens: Proverbia, quæ illi מסלי Misle, id est Parabolas appellant,
Quartus, Ecclesiastes, id est קוהלת Coheleth.
Quintus, Canticum canticorum, quem titulo סיר הסירים Sir hassirim prænotant.
Sextus, est דניאל Daniel.
Septimus, דברי הימים Dibre hajamim, id est Verba dierum, quod significantius Chronicon totius divinæ historiæ possumus appellare, qui liber apud nos Paralipomenon primus et secundus inscribitur.
Octavus עזרא Esdras, : qui et ipse similiter apud Græcos et Latinos in duos libros divisus est.
Nonus, אסתר Esther.
Atque ita fiunt pariter Veteris legis libri viginti duo : id est Moysi quinque, et Prophetarum octo, Hagiographorum novem. Quamquam nonnulli רות וקינות Ruth et Cinoth, inter Hagiographa scriptitent, et libros hos in suo putent numero supputandos : ac per hoc esse priscæ legis libros vigintiquattuor : quos sub numero viginti quattuor seniorum Apocalypsis Joannis inducit adorantes Agnum, et coronas suas prostratis vultibus offerentes : stantibus coram quattuor animalibus oculatis ante et retro, id est et in præteritum, et in futurum respicientibus, et indefessa voce clamantibus: Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Dominus Deus omnipotens, qui erat, et qui est, et qui futurus est.
Hic prologus Scripturarum quasi galeatum principium, omnibus libris quos de hebraeo vertimus in latinum, convenire potest : ut scire valeamus, quicquid extra hos est, inter apocrypha esse seponendum. Igitur Sapientia, quae vulgo Salomonis inscribitur, et Jesu filii Sirach liber, et Judith, et Tobias, et Pastor, non sunt in canone. Machabæorum primum librum, hebraicum reperi. Secundus, Græcus est : quod et ex ipsa phrasi probari potest. Quæ cum ita se habeant, obsecro te Lector, ne laborem meum, reprehensionem existimes antiquorum. In templo Dei offert unusquisque quod potest : alii aurum, argentum et lapides pretiosos : alii byssum, et purpuram et coccum offerunt et hyacinthum : nobiscum bene agitur, si obtulerimus pelles et caprarum pilos. Et tamen Apostolus contemptibiliora nostra magis necessaria judicat. Unde et tota illa tabernaculi pulchritudo, et per singulas species, Ecclesiæ praesentis futuræque distinctio, pellibus tegitur et ciliciis ardoremque solis et injuriam imbrium ea quæ viliora sunt, prohibent. Lege ergo primum Samuel, et Melachim meum : meum, inquam, meum. Quidquid enim crebrius vertendo, et emendando sollicitius et didicimus et tenemus, nostrum est. Et cum intellexeris quod antea nesciebas, vel interpretem me æstimato, si gratus es; vel Paraphrasten, si ingratus, quamquam mihi omnino conscius non sim, mutasse me quippiam de Hebraica veritate. Certe si incredulus es, lege Græcos codices et Latinos, et confer cum iis opusculis quæ nuper emendavimus : et ubicumque discrepare inter se videris, interroga quemlibet Hebræorum, cui magis accomodare debeas fidem : et si nostra firmaverit, puto quòd eum non æstimes conjectorem, ut in eodem loco mecum similiter divinarit.
Sed et vos famulas Christi rogo (quæ Domini discumbentis pretiosissima fidei myrrha ungitis caput, quæ nequaquam Salvatorem quæritis in sepulchro, quibus jam ad Patrem Christus ascendit), ut contra latrantes canes, qui adversum me rabido ore desæviunt, et circumeunt civitatem ; atque in eo se doctos arbitrantur si aliis detrahant, orationum vestrarum clypeos opponatis. Ego sciens humilitatem meam, illius semper sententiae recordabor, Dixi, custodiam vias meas : ut non delinquam in lingua mea [Psal. 38]. Posui ori meo custodiam, cum consisteret peccator adversum me; obmutui, et humiliatus sum : et silui a bonis.
thought_title: The twenty-two Hebrew letters and the twenty-two books of the Old Testament
orientation: Jerome opens his preface by explaining that the Hebrew alphabet has twenty-two letters and that the Hebrew canon of the Old Testament likewise consists of twenty-two books, which he then lists in their Hebrew order.
pass_a_gloss:
Twenty and two letters to be among [the] Hebrews, [the] language also of [the] Syrians and of [the] Chaldeans testifies, which [is] to [the] Hebrew in great part near. For also they twenty-two elements have [with] same sound, but [with] different characters. [The] Samaritans also [the] Pentateuch of Moses [with] just as many letters write repeatedly, [in] figures only and points differing. And certain it is [that] Ezra [the] scribe, and [the] law's teacher, after [the] captured Jerusalem and [the] restoration of [the] temple under Zerubbabel, other letters to have found which now we use, when unto that until time [the] same of [the] Samaritans and of [the] Hebrews characters had been. In [the] book also of Numbers this same reckoning, under [the] Levites', and [the] priests' census, mystically is shown. And [the] name of [the] Lord tetragrammaton, in certain Greek volumes, until today [with] ancient expressed letters we find. But also [the] psalms, [the] thirty-sixth, and [the] hundred [and] tenth, and [the] hundred [and] eleventh, and [the] hundred [and] eighteenth, and [the] hundred [and] forty-fourth, although [in] different they be written meter, yet of [the] same number are woven [with] alphabet. And [of] Jeremiah [the] lamentations, and [the] prayer of him: [of] Solomon also in [the] end proverbs, from that place in which he says: A strong woman who will find? [with] [the] same alphabets or divisions are reckoned. Moreover five letters double among [the] Hebrews are, Caph, Mem, Nun, Pe, Sade, for otherwise they are written through these [for] beginnings, and middles of words, otherwise [for] ends. Whence also five by most books, double are considered, Samuel, Melachim, Dibre haiamim, Esdras, Jeremias, with Cinoth, that is, [the] lamentations of him. In what way therefore twenty-two elements are, through which we write [in] Hebrew everything that we speak, and [by] their beginnings [the] voice human is comprehended: so twenty-two volumes are reckoned, [by] which as [by] letters and beginnings in [the] teaching of God, [the] tender still and suckling of [the] just man is instructed infancy. First among them [the] book, is called בראסית Beresith: which we Genesis call. Second, ואלה סמות Veelle semoth: which Exodus is called. Third, ויקרא Vaiicra, that is Leviticus. Fourth, וידבר Vajedabber, which Numbers we call. Fifth, אלה הדברים Elle haddebarim, which Deuteronomy is entitled. These are [the] five books of Moses, which properly תורה Thora, that is Law they call. Second, [the] prophets' order they make: and they begin from Jesus [the] son of Nave: who among them יהוסע בן נון Josue ben Nun is said. Then they subjoin סופטים Sophetim, that is [the] Judges book. And into [the] same they press Ruth: because in [the] days of [the] Judges [the] done of her is narrated history. Third follows סמואל Samuel, which we [the] Kings first and second call. Fourth מלכים Melachim, that is [the] Kings, which ממלכות Mamlachot, that is [the] Kingdoms to say. For not of many nations it describes [the] kingdoms, but of [the] one Israelite people, which [by] tribes twelve is contained. Fifth, is יסעיה Isaias. Sixth, ירמיה Jeremias. Seventh, יחזקאל Ezechiel. Eighth, [the] book of [the] twelve Prophets, which among them is called תרי עסר There asar. [The] third order, [the] Hagiographa possesses. And [the] first book begins from איוב Job. Second from דוד David: which [with] five divisions, and [with] one of [the] Psalms volume they comprehend. Third is סלמה Salomon, three books having: Proverbs, which they מסלי Misle, that is Parables call, Fourth, Ecclesiastes, that is קוהלת Coheleth. Fifth, [the] Canticle of canticles, which [with] title סיר הסירים Sir hassirim they entitle. Sixth, is דניאל Daniel. Seventh, דברי הימים Dibre hajamim, that is Words of days, which more significantly [the] Chronicle of [the] whole divine history we can call, which book among us Paralipomenon first and second is inscribed. Eighth עזרא Esdras, which also itself similarly among [the] Greeks and Latins into two books [has been] divided. Ninth, אסתר Esther. And so there become equally of [the] Old law [the] books twenty-two: that is of Moses five, and of [the] Prophets eight, of [the] Hagiographa nine. Although some רות וקינות Ruth and Cinoth, among [the] Hagiographa write repeatedly, and [the] books these [in] their own think number to be reckoned: and through this to be of [the] ancient law [the] books twenty-four: which under [the] number of [the] twenty-four elders [the] Apocalypse of John leads in adoring [the] Lamb, and [the] crowns of them [with] prostrated faces offering: [with] standing before [the] four animals eyed before and behind, that is both into [the] past, and into [the] future looking, and [with] unwearied voice crying: Holy, holy, holy Lord God almighty, who was, and who is, and who [is] about to be. This prologue of [the] Scriptures as [a] helmeted beginning, to all [the] books which from [the] Hebrew we have turned into Latin, to be fitting can: so that to know we may be able, whatever outside these is, among [the] apocrypha to be set aside. Therefore [the] Wisdom, which commonly of Solomon is inscribed, and of Jesus [the] son of Sirach [the] book, and Judith, and Tobias, and [the] Pastor, not are in [the] canon. [The] Maccabees' first book, Hebrew I found. [The] second, Greek is: which also from [the] phrase itself to be proved can. Which when so themselves have, I beseech you Reader, [do] not [consider] my labor [a] reproach of [the] ancients. In [the] temple of God offers each one what he can: some gold, silver and stones precious: others fine linen, and purple and scarlet offer and hyacinth: with us well it is done, if we have offered skins and of goats hairs. And yet [the] Apostle [the] more contemptible things of us more necessary judges. Whence also all that of [the] tabernacle beauty, and through [the] single kinds, of [the] Church [of the] present and [of the] future [the] distinction, [with] skins is covered and [with] haircloths, and [the] heat of [the] sun and [the] injury of rains those which [are] cheaper, keep off. Read therefore first Samuel, and Melachim mine: mine, I say, mine. For whatever [by] more frequently translating, and [by] emending more carefully both we have learned and we hold, ours is. And when you have understood what before you did not know, either [as] translator me consider, if grateful you are; or [as] Paraphrast, if ungrateful, although to me entirely conscious I am not, [that] I have changed anything of [the] Hebrew truth. Certainly if unbelieving you are, read [the] Greek codices and Latin, and compare with those little works which lately we have emended: and wherever to differ among themselves you see, ask any of [the] Hebrews, to whom more you ought to accommodate faith: and if our [things] he has confirmed, I think that you [will] not consider him [a] guesser, as in [the] same place with me similarly he has divined.
But also you [the] handmaids of Christ I ask (who [with the] most precious myrrh of faith of [the] Lord reclining [at table] anoint [the] head, who by no means [the] Savior seek in [the] tomb, [to] whom already to [the] Father Christ has ascended), that against [the] barking dogs, who against me [with] rabid mouth rage, and go around [the] city; and in this [thing] themselves learned they judge if [to] others they detract, [the] shields of your prayers you may oppose. I knowing my humility, of that always sentence I will remember, I said, I will guard my ways: that not I may transgress in my tongue [Psal. 38]. I set [to] my mouth a guard, when stood [the] sinner against me; I was silent, and I was humbled: and I was silent from good [things].

choices.english: with the most precious myrrh of faith
choices.why: The myrrh is the instrument of anointing; 'most precious' renders the superlative, and 'of faith' keeps the genitive as a defining quality.
rejected: with the precious myrrh of faith

choices.why: A literal rendering of the insult; 'barking' keeps the animal imagery of noisy, aggressive detractors.
Rabidus means raging or mad; 'rabid' preserves the disease-like fury of the critics' speech.
The metaphor of prayer as defensive armor is kept literally; 'shields' is the concrete image Jerome uses.

choices.english: I kept silent from good things
choices.why: The Psalm phrase is rendered literally; 'from good things' preserves the oddness of the Hebrew idiom that Jerome quotes, where silence is abstention even from good speech.
rejected: I was silent about good things
I held my peace even from good

bible_refs.note: Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Dominus Deus omnipotens, qui erat, et qui est, et qui futurus est.
Dixi, custodiam vias meas : ut non delinquam in lingua mea. Posui ori meo custodiam, cum consisteret peccator adversum me; obmutui, et humiliatus sum : et silui a bonis.

pass_b_english: That the Hebrews have twenty-two letters is attested also by the language of the Syrians and the Chaldeans, which is for the most part close to Hebrew. For they too have twenty-two elements with the same sound, but different characters. The Samaritans also habitually write the Law of Moses with the same number of letters, differing only in shapes and points. And it is certain that Ezra the scribe, the teacher of the Law, after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel, discovered other letters which we now use, since up to that time the characters of the Samaritans and the Hebrews had been the same. In the book of Numbers also this same reckoning is mystically shown under the census of the Levites and priests.

And we find the name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, in certain Greek volumes even to this day expressed in the ancient letters. But also Psalms 36, 110, 111, 118, and 144, although they are written in different meter, are nevertheless woven together by the alphabet of the same number. And the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and his prayer, and also the Proverbs of Solomon at the end, from the place where he says, “A capable wife who can find?” (Proverbs 31:10), are reckoned by the same alphabets or sections. Moreover, there are five double letters among the Hebrews: Caph, Mem, Nun, Pe, Sade. For they are written one way through these at the beginnings and middles of words, and another way at the ends. Hence also five books are considered double by most: Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, and Jeremiah with Lamentations, that is, with his Lamentations. Therefore, just as there are twenty-two elements by which we write in Hebrew everything that we speak, and by their beginnings human speech is comprehended, so twenty-two volumes are reckoned, by which, as if by letters and beginnings in the teaching of God, the tender and still nursing infancy of a righteous man is instructed.
The first book among them is called Beresith, which we call Genesis.
The second, Veelle semoth, which is called Exodus.
The third, Vaiicra, that is, Leviticus.
The fourth, Vajedabber, which we call Numbers.
The fifth, Elle haddebarim, which is entitled Deuteronomy. These are the five books of Moses, which they properly call Thora, that is, the Law.
They make the second order of the Prophets, and they begin with Joshua son of Nun, who among them is called Joshua son of Nun.
Then they attach Judges, that is, the book of Judges. And they join Ruth into the same book, because her history is narrated as taking place in the days of the Judges.
The third follows, Samuel, which we call the first and second books of Kings.

The fourth is Melachim, that is, of Kings, rather than Mamlachot, that is, of Kingdoms. For it does not describe the kingdoms of many nations, but of the one Israelite people, which is contained in twelve tribes.
The fifth is Isaiah.
The sixth, Jeremiah.
The seventh, Ezekiel.
The eighth, the book of the Twelve Prophets, which among them is called There asar.
The third order holds the Writings.
And the first book begins with Job.
The second with David, whom they comprise in five sections and one volume of Psalms.
The third is Solomon, having three books: Proverbs, which they call Misle, that is, Parables.
The fourth, Ecclesiastes, that is, Coheleth.
The fifth, Song of Songs, which they entitle Sir hassirim.
The sixth is Daniel.

The seventh, Dibre hajamim, that is, Words of Days, which we can more significantly call the Chronicle of the whole divine history, which book among us is inscribed as the first and second books of Chronicles.
The eighth, Esdras, which also itself is similarly divided into two books among the Greeks and Latins.
The ninth, Esther.

And so there are together twenty-two books of the Old Law: that is, five of Moses, eight of the Prophets, and nine of the Writings. Although some write Ruth and Lamentations among the Writings, and think these books should be reckoned in their own number, and therefore there are twenty-four books of the ancient Law: whom the Apocalypse of John introduces under the number of the twenty-four elders worshiping the Lamb, and offering their crowns with faces cast down, while standing before the four living creatures, which are full of eyes before and behind—that is, looking both to the past and to the future—and crying out with unwearied voice: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come” (Revelation 4:8).

This prologue of the Scriptures, like a helmeted beginning, can be suitable for all the books which we have translated from Hebrew into Latin, so that we may know that whatever is outside these is to be set aside among the apocryphal books. Therefore Wisdom, which is commonly inscribed as Solomon's, and the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and Judith, and Tobias, and the Shepherd, are not in the canon. I have found the first book of Maccabees in Hebrew. The second is Greek, which can also be proved from its very style. Since these things are so, I beg you, reader, not to consider my labor a reproach of the ancients. In the temple of God each one offers what he can: some offer gold, silver, and precious stones; others offer fine linen, purple, scarlet, and hyacinth. It goes well with us if we offer skins and goat hair. And yet the Apostle judges our more contemptible things more necessary. Hence also all that beauty of the tabernacle, and its distinction into each kind of the present and future Church, is covered with skins and haircloths, and the cheaper things keep off the heat of the sun and the injury of rain. Read then my Samuel and Kings: mine, I say, mine. For whatever we have learned and hold by translating more frequently and emending more carefully is ours. And when you understand what you did not know before, consider me either a translator, if you are grateful, or a paraphraser, if you are ungrateful—although I am not at all conscious to myself that I have changed anything from the original Hebrew. Certainly if you are incredulous, read the Greek and Latin codices, and compare them with these little works which we have recently emended: and wherever you see them disagree among themselves, ask any of the Hebrews to whom you should rather give credence: and if he confirms our version, I think you will not consider him a guesser, as if he had divined in the same place as I did.

But I also ask you, handmaids of Christ—you who anoint the head of the Lord reclining at table with the most precious myrrh of faith, who do not seek the Savior in the tomb, since Christ has already ascended to the Father—to set the shields of your prayers against the barking dogs who rage against me with rabid mouth and go around the city, and who think themselves learned if they disparage others. Knowing my own lowliness, I will always remember that saying: I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue (Psalm 39 [Hebrew]; 38 in the Septuagint/Vulgate numbering). I set a guard on my mouth when the sinner stood against me; I was mute and humbled, and I kept silent from good things.

problems.source_quote: Primus apud eos liber, vocatur בראסית Beresith : quem nos Genesim dicimus.
problems.why: Source says 'among them' (apud eos) Hebrews call it Beresith, 'which we call Genesis'; English reverses to 'called Genesis, which we call Genesis', losing Hebrew name.
problems.fix: The first book among them is called Beresith, which we call Genesis.

problems.quote: I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue (Psalm 38:1). I set a guard on my mouth when the sinner stood against me; I was mute and humbled, and I kept silent from good things (Psalm 38:2-3).
problems.source_quote: Dixi, custodiam vias meas : ut non delinquam in lingua mea [Psal. 38]. Posui ori meo custodiam, cum consisteret peccator adversum me; obmutui, et humiliatus sum : et silui a bonis.
problems.why: Jerome cites Psalm 38 (Hebrew numbering), which is Psalm 39 in LXX/Vulgate; English gives 'Psalm 38' with verse numbers 1, 2-3, but these verse numbers follow Hebrew numbering. Per brief, should note Hebrew numbering. However, the brief says 'Citations should be given in modern form with Hebrew Psalm numbering, e.g. Psalm 38 (Hebrew) = Psalm 39 (LXX/Vulgate).' The English gives 'Psalm 38:1' and 'Psalm 38:2-3' without indicating Hebrew numbering. But is this wrong? The brief says 'Psalms are numbered according to the Hebrew text, which Jerome follows; in the preface he cites Psalm 38 (Hebrew numbering)... Citations should be given in modern form with Hebrew Psalm numbering.' So 'Psalm 38' alone is ambiguous—readers may think LXX/Vulgate 38. Should be 'Psalm 38 (Hebrew)' or equivalent. This is a wrong_scripture issue per brief instructions.
problems.fix: I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue (Psalm 38 [Hebrew]). I set a guard on my mouth when the sinner stood against me; I was mute and humbled, and I kept silent from good things.
problems.ruling: Source says '[Psal. 38]'; English adds ':1' and ':2-3' without noting Hebrew numbering, risking reader confusion with LXX/Vulgate 38.

problems.quote: which they call Mamlachot, that is, of Kingdoms
problems.source_quote: Melachim, id est Regum, quam ממלכות Mamlachot, id est Regnorum dicere.
problems.why: 'quam...dicere' means 'rather than to say Kingdoms'. Jerome says the book should be called Kings, not Kingdoms. The English presents Kingdoms as the Hebrew name, which contradicts the 'For it does not describe...' explanation.
problems.fix: The fourth is Melachim, that is, of Kings, rather than Mamlachot, that is, of Kingdoms. For it does not describe the kingdoms of many nations, but of the one Israelite people.

problems.quote: while standing before the four living creatures full of eyes before and behind, that is, looking both to the past and to the future, and crying out with unwearied voice
problems.source_quote: stantibus coram quattuor animalibus oculatis ante et retro, id est et in praeteritum, et in futurum respicientibus, et indefessa voce clamantibus
problems.why: Eyes, the look to past and future, and the Holy cry belong to the four creatures, not the elders.
problems.fix: standing before the four living creatures, eyed before and behind—that is, looking to past and future—and crying with unwearied voice
problems.ruling: "stantibus coram quattuor animalibus oculatis... respicientibus... clamantibus": the creatures are eyed, look both ways and cry; English 'whom... elders' and 'while standing before' garble the agency, though participles may attach to elders.

last_rejected.quote: Samuel, which we call the first and second books of Kings

last_rejected.quote: Melachim, that is, of Kings, which they call Mamlachot, that is, of Kingdoms

last_rejected.fix: Melachim, that is, of Kings, which to call Mamlachot, that is, of Kingdoms
last_rejected.ruling: 'dicere' governs both Hebrew names; 'they call' is normal rendering, no meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: Esdras, which also itself is similarly divided into two books among the Greeks and Latins

last_rejected.fix: Esdras, which also itself is similarly divided into two books among the Greeks and Latins

last_rejected.ruling: 'ea quæ viliora sunt' refers back to skins/haircloths; 'cheaper things' is accurate, no error.

last_rejected.fix: I am not at all conscious to myself that I have changed anything from the Hebrew truth

last_rejected.quote: as if he had divined in the same place as I did

last_rejected.ruling: 'silui a bonis' = 'kept silent from good things'; accurate rendering of Psalm 38:10, no real error.

last_rejected.source_quote: psalmi, trigesimus sextus, et centesimus decimus, et centesimus undecimus, et centesimus decimus octavus, et centesimus quadragesimus quartus
last_rejected.why: These Latin numbers are LXX/Vulgate acrostics; Hebrew numbering is 37, 111, 112, 119, and 145.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin numbers 'trigesimus sextus... centesimus decimus' are Vulgate numbering; Jerome's text uses it. Translator keeping source numbers is faithful, though a note might help; not meaning-changing.

last_rejected.quote: while standing before the four living creatures, which are full of eyes before and behind—that is, looking both to the past and to the future—and crying out with unwearied voice
last_rejected.source_quote: stantibus coram quattuor animalibus oculatis ante et retro, id est et in præteritum, et in futurum respicientibus, et indefessa voce clamantibus
last_rejected.why: The creatures stand, look both ways, and cry the sanctus; the elders worship and offer crowns.
last_rejected.fix: offering their crowns with faces cast down before the four living creatures, which stand, eyed before and behind—looking to past and future—and cry with unwearied voice
last_rejected.ruling: English 'standing before the four living creatures... crying out' is ambiguous but the ablative absolutes 'stantibus... clamantibus' plausibly refer to the elders; the English follows the source's looseness.

last_rejected.quote: and its distinction into each kind of the present and future Church
last_rejected.source_quote: et per singulas species, Ecclesiæ praesentis futuræque distinctio

last_rejected.fix: and, in each detail, the distinction of the present and future Church
last_rejected.ruling: 'distinction into each kind of the present and future Church' fairly renders 'per singulas species, Ecclesiae praesentis futuraeque distinctio'; the claim is only a phrasing preference.

last_rejected.quote: wherever you see them disagree among themselves

last_rejected.ruling: 'discrepare inter se' means the copies disagree among themselves; the comparison clause 'confer cum iis opusculis' already conveys the revised works, so English is acceptable.
